h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Filling an empty input edge with a conv restores the path feeding edges 2 and 4, gaining more than swapping an existing op.
Adding a conv on an empty edge into the output gains more than swapping one existing op for another.
Adding a strong conv to an empty slot gains more than replacing an existing op.
Filling an empty output edge with a conv gains more than replacing an existing op.
Reconnecting a disconnected input edge restores flow into nodes 1, 2 and 3, which matters more than swapping ops.
Removing a strong conv from the output edge hurts more than removing a weaker op.
Removing a conv from the critical input edge hurts more than removing a weak op.
Deleting a strong conv costs more accuracy than deleting a weaker op.
Filling the empty 0->3 edge with a conv adds a useful output path, whereas replacing an existing op changes less.
Adding a conv to an empty slot gains more than replacing an existing op.
